hints: Look closely at how endocytosis and exocytosis move things, in vesicles made from membrane, not through a tiny channel or carrier protein.
Ask yourself if a process that uses ATP to wrap up bulk material in a vesicle needs to wait for diffusion down a concentration gradient.
walkthrough:
**Picture what bulk transport is**

Think of endocytosis as the cell membrane wrapping around material outside and pinching off a vesicle inside. Think of exocytosis as a vesicle inside fusing with the membrane to release material outside.

It is bulk movement, not single molecules slipping through.

**Check the role of the concentration gradient**

Diffusion and facilitated diffusion depend on going from higher to lower concentration. Endocytosis and exocytosis do not.

They are active processes using ATP for membrane movement and vesicle formation, so they can move material up a gradient, down a gradient, or when concentrations are equal.

**Match this to the table**

For endocytosis (outside to inside), the substance outside could be equal, higher, or lower than inside. For exocytosis (inside to outside), the same is true.

Only row B allows all three possibilities for both processes.

options.A: Too restrictive. Bulk transport does not only happen when concentrations are equal, it can happen against a gradient too.
options.B: Correct. Both endocytosis and exocytosis use ATP and vesicles, so they are independent of the gradient and work whether concentrations are equal, greater inside, or greater outside.
options.C: Applies diffusion logic. It wrongly suggests endocytosis only works down a gradient into the cell and exocytosis only works down a gradient out of the cell.
options.D: Also applies diffusion logic but reversed. It wrongly limits each process to only some gradient conditions instead of all conditions.
